title: Neoplasms of the Pulmonary System and Upper Respiratory Tract
subject: Respiratory System (RESP)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter covers tumors and tumor-like masses from the nose to the pleura, together with esophageal cancer, which lies beside the trachea and shares its late complications. For each lesion it explains the cell of origin, the cause, and how location and secretory behavior produce the findings. Board questions usually give a location, a smoking history, a histologic or marker finding, or a paraneoplastic laboratory pattern and ask for the tumor type, or describe a hoarse voice, a drooping eyelid, or a swollen face and ask which structure the tumor has invaded. If you can trace each finding back to the cell type and its anatomic neighbors, most of these questions resolve.
prerequisites: Histology of the respiratory tract epithelium from nasal cavity to alveolus, including neuroendocrine cells and type II pneumocytes
Metaplasia, dysplasia, carcinoma in situ, and invasion (general neoplasia)
Tumor suppressor genes TP53 and RB1 and the oncogenic proteins E6 and E7 of HPV
Anatomy of the mediastinum, thoracic inlet, larynx, and nasopharynx, including the phrenic and recurrent laryngeal nerves
Endocrine control of calcium (PTH), cortisol (ACTH), and water balance (ADH)

connections.to: Disorders of the pleural cavity and lung expansion (PU-14-D)
connections.how: Malignant pleural effusion, atelectasis from bronchial obstruction, and asbestos-related pleural plaques are the pleural and expansion consequences of the tumors in this chapter.

connections.to: Diseases of the upper respiratory tract (PU-14-C)
connections.how: Chronic rhinosinusitis, otitis media, and laryngeal inflammation must be separated from polyps, nasopharyngeal carcinoma, and laryngeal tumors that mimic them.
Esophageal carcinoma and the gut carcinoid are treated with the digestive tract; this chapter explains their thoracic and airway effects and why bronchial carcinoids differ.
Ectopic ACTH, ADH, and PTHrP from lung cancers are major causes of Cushing syndrome, SIADH, and hypercalcemia of malignancy.
Lambert-Eaton syndrome, Horner syndrome, and brachial plexus deficits connect lung tumors to the neuromuscular junction and the peripheral and autonomic nervous systems.

terms.def: Growth of tumor cells along the surface of intact alveolar walls without destroying the alveolar architecture.

Indentation of one nucleus by its neighbor, seen when cells with scant cytoplasm are packed tightly, as in small cell carcinoma.
A concentric whorl of keratinized squamous cells within a tumor, a sign of squamous differentiation.
Desmosomal junctions between squamous cells, visible by light microscopy as fine spines crossing the space between cells.
Signs and symptoms produced at a distance by tumor-derived hormones, cytokines, or autoantibodies rather than by local invasion or metastasis.
Replacement of the distal esophageal squamous epithelium by intestinal-type columnar epithelium with goblet cells, a response to chronic reflux.
A carcinoma of the lung apex that invades the thoracic inlet structures, including the lower brachial plexus and cervical sympathetic chain.
A single round opacity of 3 cm or less completely surrounded by lung tissue.
Widespread carcinogen-induced genetic damage across an exposed mucosal surface, which favors multiple precursor lesions and separate primary tumors.
An HPV-infected squamous cell with a wrinkled nucleus and a clear perinuclear halo.
The most common benign lung tumor, composed mainly of mature cartilage and fat, now known to be a clonal neoplasm.

blocks.text: In the lung, the cell of origin largely decides where a tumor sits, what it looks like, and how it behaves. Adenocarcinoma is a malignant tumor with glandular differentiation that arises from the peripheral bronchiolar and alveolar epithelium, including club cells and type II pneumocytes. It accounts for about 40% or more of lung cancers, making it the most common type overall, and it is the most common type in women and in people who have never smoked. Even so, most adenocarcinomas occur in smokers.

Because it arises in the periphery, adenocarcinoma usually presents as a peripheral nodule or mass rather than as a central airway lesion and causes cough and hemoptysis later than central tumors do. It also reaches the pleura readily, a common source of malignant effusion. Histologically the tumor forms glands, papillae, or solid sheets, and the cells produce mucin, which stains with mucicarmine or periodic acid-Schiff. Most express TTF-1 (thyroid transcription factor 1) and napsin A, which help confirm a lung primary.

The molecular profile differs with smoking history. Tumors in never smokers more often carry activating mutations of EGFR (epidermal growth factor receptor), especially in East Asian women, or rearrangements of ALK, whereas tumors in smokers more often carry KRAS mutations. Each of these keeps growth factor signaling switched on without a ligand.
Adenocarcinoma in situ

Peripheral adenocarcinoma is thought to develop stepwise, as shown below. Adenocarcinoma in situ (AIS), previously included under the term bronchioloalveolar carcinoma, is a lesion of 3 cm or less in which atypical cells grow purely along intact alveolar walls, the pattern called lepidic growth. The alveolar framework is preserved and there is no stromal, vascular, or pleural invasion, so the lesion cannot metastasize and its prognosis is excellent.

Because AIS lines alveoli without filling them, the alveoli still contain air, and on CT the lesion appears as a hazy ground-glass opacity; as invasion and stromal fibrosis develop, a solid component appears. Mucinous tumors can spread through the airspaces and produce consolidation that resembles a pneumonia that does not resolve.

blocks.title: Stepwise progression of peripheral adenocarcinoma
steps: Atypical adenomatous hyperplasia: atypical alveolar lining cells, 5 mm or less
Adenocarcinoma in situ: pure lepidic growth, 3 cm or less
Minimally invasive adenocarcinoma: invasive focus 5 mm or less
Invasive adenocarcinoma: stromal, vascular, or pleural invasion
blocks.caption: Lepidic growth preserves alveolar walls and air; invasion destroys them and allows metastasis.

blocks.text: Neuroendocrine cells are scattered through the bronchial epithelium and contain dense-core granules that store amines and peptides. Tumors of these cells form a spectrum graded by mitotic rate and necrosis: typical carcinoid (low grade), atypical carcinoid (intermediate grade), and the high-grade large cell neuroendocrine carcinoma and small cell carcinoma. Bronchial carcinoid sits at the low-grade end. It accounts for only a few percent of lung tumors, tends to affect younger adults than other lung cancers, and has no established link to smoking.

Microscopically, typical carcinoid consists of nests, cords, or ribbons of uniform cells with round nuclei, finely granular chromatin, few mitoses, and no necrosis. The cells are positive for chromogranin and synaptophysin, reflecting their secretory granules, and electron microscopy shows dense-core neurosecretory granules. Atypical carcinoid has more mitoses or foci of necrosis and metastasizes more often.

Most arise in main or lobar bronchi as a fleshy, polypoid mass covered by intact mucosa, and symptoms come from the mass rather than from hormones. Partial obstruction causes cough, localized wheeze, and recurrent pneumonia in the same segment, complete obstruction causes collapse (atelectasis) of the lung beyond it, and the vascular surface causes hemoptysis. Typical carcinoids grow slowly and seldom metastasize.

Carcinoid syndrome is the systemic effect of secreted serotonin, kinins, and other vasoactive products: episodic flushing, diarrhea, and bronchospasm. It is rare with bronchial carcinoids because most secrete little. Venous drainage also matters. Products of a gut carcinoid enter the portal vein and are inactivated in the liver, so the syndrome there usually requires liver metastases. Blood from a lung tumor returns largely through the pulmonary veins to the left heart without passing the liver, so a large secreting bronchial carcinoid can cause the syndrome without liver involvement, and rare valve fibrosis then favors the left side. Urinary 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA), the main serotonin metabolite, rises when the syndrome is present.

blocks.title: Two neuroendocrine lung tumors
rows: Uniform, moderate cytoplasm, nests and ribbons

Central mass with bulky nodes, paraneoplastic syndromes
blocks.caption: Both share neuroendocrine markers, so grade, cell appearance, and behavior separate them.

blocks.text: The esophagus runs through the posterior mediastinum directly behind the trachea and left main bronchus, so its cancers have respiratory complications. The esophagus is lined by nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium, and its two main cancers reflect two kinds of injury. Squamous cell carcinoma arises from the native squamous lining; adenocarcinoma arises from columnar epithelium that has replaced the squamous lining in the distal esophagus. Squamous cell carcinoma is more common worldwide, whereas adenocarcinoma is now the more common type in the United States and other Western countries.

Squamous cell carcinoma develops through squamous dysplasia after long chemical and thermal injury, mostly in the upper and middle thirds. Tobacco and alcohol act together: alcohol dissolves tobacco carcinogens and its metabolite acetaldehyde is mutagenic. Very hot beverages cause repeated thermal injury, and dietary nitrosamines alkylate DNA. In achalasia, failure of the lower esophageal sphincter to relax leaves food stagnant in a dilated esophagus, keeping the mucosa chronically irritated; caustic (lye) strictures carry a similar risk.

Adenocarcinoma follows chronic gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD). Repeated exposure to acid and bile causes the distal squamous lining to be replaced by intestinal-type columnar epithelium with goblet cells, Barrett esophagus. The metaplasia is an adaptation, but the new cells can accumulate mutations such as TP53 and progress through dysplasia to invasive carcinoma, so these tumors arise in the distal third and near the gastroesophageal junction. Obesity increases risk by promoting reflux, and white men are affected most.

Both types cause the same mechanical symptoms. A growing mass narrows the lumen, so dysphagia is progressive, first for solids and later for liquids, and weight loss follows reduced intake and tumor catabolism. Most of the esophagus is covered by adventitia rather than serosa, so there is no barrier to local spread, and its rich submucosal lymphatics allow early nodal spread. A tumor that erodes into the trachea or left main bronchus creates a tracheoesophageal fistula: swallowed food and liquid enter the airway, causing cough with swallowing and recurrent aspiration pneumonia. Invasion of the left recurrent laryngeal nerve adds hoarseness.

blocks.title: Squamous cell carcinoma versus adenocarcinoma of the esophagus
rows: Smoking, alcohol, very hot drinks, achalasia, nitrosamines, caustic stricture
Most common type in Western countries
blocks.caption: Both present with progressive dysphagia, weight loss, and possible tracheoesophageal fistula.

sections.title: Laryngeal carcinoma, vocal fold nodules, and papillomatosis

blocks.text: The larynx has a supraglottis (epiglottis and false vocal folds), glottis (true vocal folds), and subglottis. About 95% of laryngeal cancers are squamous cell carcinomas. They arise from the squamous epithelium of the true folds, or from squamous metaplasia elsewhere, through hyperplasia, dysplasia, and carcinoma in situ. Smoking is the dominant cause and alcohol multiplies its effect, so most patients are older men who smoke.

Glottic tumors are the most common and produce hoarseness early. Voice requires two pliable folds that meet in the midline and vibrate, and even a small tumor stiffens the mucosa and adds mass, so the folds vibrate irregularly and close incompletely, so a persistent voice change draws attention while the tumor is small. The glottis also has sparse lymphatics, so nodal metastasis comes late. Supraglottic tumors cause few early voice changes, drain into a rich lymphatic network, and often present with neck node metastases, sore throat, or pain referred to the ear. Advanced tumors fix the vocal fold and obstruct the airway, causing stridor.

Vocal fold nodules (singer's nodules) are small, usually bilateral and symmetric swellings at the junction of the anterior and middle thirds of the true folds, the point of greatest impact during vibration. They form from repeated collision of the folds in people who overuse the voice, such as singers, teachers, and children who shout, and they consist of edematous or fibrous connective tissue covered by squamous epithelium. They are reactive, not neoplastic, and they do not become malignant.

Squamous papillomas are benign tumors of the true folds caused by low-risk HPV types 6 and 11. In adults they are usually single. In children they are typically multiple and recur after removal, called juvenile (recurrent respiratory) papillomatosis, and are thought to follow transmission of the virus from the mother during birth. Each papilloma is a finger-like projection of squamous epithelium around a fibrovascular core, often with koilocytes. They cause hoarseness and can spread down the airway. Malignant change is rare because the E6 and E7 proteins of types 6 and 11 bind p53 and Rb only weakly.

blocks.title: Causes of hoarseness at the true vocal fold
rows: Usually one side; invasive, late nodal spread
blocks.caption: Hoarseness arises early at the glottis because any mass alters vocal fold vibration and closure.

blocks.text: Malignant mesothelioma is a cancer of the mesothelial cells that line the pleura (most often), the peritoneum, and the pericardium. Most cases follow occupational or environmental asbestos exposure, with a latency of several decades, usually about 25 to 45 years. Amphibole fibers such as crocidolite are long, thin, and straight; they reach the pleura and persist, and they are more carcinogenic than the curly serpentine fiber chrysotile. Persistent fibers drive chronic inflammation, reactive oxygen species, and DNA damage in mesothelial cells. Loss of the tumor suppressor BAP1 is common, and germline BAP1 mutations explain some familial cases.

Smoking multiplies the risk of lung carcinoma in asbestos-exposed workers, but it does not increase the risk of mesothelioma. Even in an asbestos-exposed smoker, lung carcinoma remains more common than mesothelioma. Pleural plaques, dense and often calcified collagen plaques on the parietal pleura, are the most common asbestos lesion; they mark exposure but are not precursors of mesothelioma. Ferruginous bodies, asbestos fibers coated with iron-containing protein, may be found in the lung.

The tumor begins as small pleural nodules that spread and fuse into a thick sheet encasing the lung like a rind and obliterating the pleural space. Patients present with chest pain from involvement of the sensitive parietal pleura, dyspnea, and a recurrent pleural effusion that is often hemorrhagic, because tumor on the pleural surface bleeds and keeps producing fluid. Histologic patterns are epithelioid (most common), sarcomatoid, and biphasic.
Mesothelioma or metastatic adenocarcinoma

Metastatic adenocarcinoma, from lung, breast, ovary, or stomach, is much more common in the pleura than mesothelioma, and both can produce bloody effusions and gland-like or papillary patterns. Cytokeratin does not separate them, because mesothelial cells are epithelial and express it too. The decision rests on lineage markers and on the shape of the cells' microvilli, as the table shows.

blocks.title: Mesothelioma versus metastatic adenocarcinoma in the pleura
rows: CEA, MOC-31, BerEP4 (TTF-1 if lung primary)
blocks.caption: Mesothelial markers and microvillus shape identify the cell of origin.

blocks.title: Worked example: identifying a pleural tumor
blocks.text: A 68-year-old retired shipyard worker who never smoked has dyspnea and a bloody right pleural effusion that returns after drainage; CT shows a thick pleural rind around the lung. Biopsy shows malignant cells forming tubules. Step 1: cytokeratin is positive, which proves only epithelial lineage, and both candidates are epithelial. Step 2: calretinin and WT1 are positive while CEA and TTF-1 are negative, which points to mesothelial cells. Step 3: electron microscopy shows long slender microvilli, a mesothelial feature, not the short stubby microvilli of glandular cells. Step 4: decades-old asbestos exposure fits, and the lack of smoking is irrelevant because smoking does not raise mesothelioma risk. Diagnosis: malignant mesothelioma. Had CEA and TTF-1 been positive with calretinin negative, the answer would be metastatic lung adenocarcinoma.

Nasopharyngeal carcinoma arises most often in the lateral recess of the nasopharynx, just behind the opening of the eustachian (auditory) tube. Its cause combines Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) infection, genetic susceptibility, and environment. Incidence is far higher in southern China, Southeast Asia, and parts of Africa (especially North Africa) than in most Western countries. In high-risk regions, eating salt-cured fish, which contains nitrosamines, from early childhood is a recognized cofactor, and certain HLA types raise susceptibility. In parts of Africa the disease also affects children and adolescents.

EBV infects nasopharyngeal epithelial cells in a latent form. Nearly every tumor cell carries the viral genome, and the viral DNA is clonal, showing that infection came before transformation. The latent protein LMP1 (latent membrane protein 1) behaves like a permanently activated CD40 receptor and switches on NF-kappaB, promoting proliferation and survival. Tumor cells contain EBV-encoded small RNAs (EBER), which can be detected by in situ hybridization.

The tumors are keratinizing squamous cell carcinomas or nonkeratinizing carcinomas, the latter subdivided into differentiated and undifferentiated forms. Nonkeratinizing and undifferentiated tumors dominate in high-incidence regions and are the most consistently EBV positive. The undifferentiated form shows large epithelial cells with vesicular nuclei and prominent nucleoli, with indistinct cell borders, mixed with many reactive lymphocytes, a pattern once called lymphoepithelioma. Cytokeratin staining identifies the malignant cells as epithelial and separates the tumor from lymphoma.

The primary tumor is often small and silent in this hidden space, so the most common presenting sign is a painless, firm, enlarging upper neck mass, because the nasopharynx drains through a rich lymphatic network to the retropharyngeal and deep cervical nodes. A tumor at the eustachian tube opening blocks ventilation of the middle ear; the mucosa absorbs the trapped gas, pressure falls, and a serous transudate fills the middle ear, causing one-sided conductive hearing loss and fullness. One-sided serous otitis media in an adult should therefore raise suspicion. Larger tumors cause nasal obstruction and bloody nasal discharge, and invasion of the skull base can produce cranial nerve palsies.

sections.title: Nasal polyps and vocal fold polyps

blocks.text: Nasal and vocal fold polyps are inflammatory or reactive projections of mucosa, not neoplasms, but they are the most common upper airway masses and must be separated from tumors.

Nasal polyps are smooth, pale, grape-like, edematous outgrowths of the sinonasal mucosa, usually bilateral and arising mainly from the ethmoid sinuses and middle meatus. They consist of loose, edematous stroma covered by respiratory epithelium with a thickened basement membrane and an inflammatory infiltrate that in most adults is rich in eosinophils. They develop in chronic rhinosinusitis, often with allergy or asthma, especially with type 2 inflammation, in which IL-4, IL-5, and IL-13 recruit eosinophils and increase vascular permeability, so fluid collects in the lamina propria and the mucosa sags into the nasal cavity.

Aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease combines asthma, chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps, and respiratory reactions to aspirin and other COX-1 inhibitors. These patients overproduce cysteinyl leukotrienes and depend on prostaglandin E2 to restrain their mast cells and leukotriene synthesis, so blocking COX-1 sets off the sequence below.

blocks.title: Aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease
steps: Aspirin or another NSAID inhibits COX-1
Prostaglandin E2 falls, removing its brake on mast cells
Arachidonic acid shifts to the 5-lipoxygenase pathway
Cysteinyl leukotrienes and mast cell mediators surge
Bronchospasm, nasal congestion, and rhinorrhea follow within hours
blocks.caption: The reaction is not IgE mediated; it results from altered arachidonic acid metabolism.

blocks.text: Nasal polyps are unusual in children, and their presence should prompt evaluation for cystic fibrosis. Defective CFTR chloride transport makes sinus mucus thick and poorly cleared, leading to chronic infection and neutrophil-rich inflammation. A single, one-sided nasal mass, especially with bleeding, does not fit an inflammatory polyp and raises concern for a tumor.

Polyps obstruct the nasal airway, causing congestion and mouth breathing, and block sinus openings, predisposing to recurrent sinusitis. Anosmia (loss of smell) results mainly because polyps prevent odorant-carrying air from reaching the olfactory epithelium in the roof of the nasal cavity, with inflammation of the olfactory mucosa adding a sensory component.

Vocal fold polyps form on the free edge of a true vocal fold, usually on one side, after vocal strain such as shouting or chronic irritation from smoking. Shearing forces injure small vessels in the superficial lamina propria, and the edema or hemorrhage organizes into a soft polyp that keeps the folds from closing evenly and disturbs their vibration, causing hoarseness or a breathy voice. In heavy smokers, diffuse bilateral swelling of the superficial lamina propria (polypoid degeneration) lowers the pitch of the voice.

blocks.title: Benign upper airway masses
rows: Chronic rhinosinusitis, atopy, asthma, aspirin-exacerbated disease, cystic fibrosis in a child
Free edge of one true fold
Junction of anterior and middle thirds of true folds
blocks.caption: A one-sided nasal mass or a nasal polyp in a child is atypical and needs further explanation.

blocks.text: Small cell carcinoma is a high-grade neuroendocrine carcinoma that makes up about 15% of lung cancers. It is the type most strongly tied to smoking, since nearly all patients are current or former heavy smokers. It usually arises centrally in the major bronchi and spreads in the bronchial wall and peribronchial tissue, so it often appears as a large hilar and mediastinal mass with bulky nodes rather than an endobronchial polyp.

The cells are small, usually less than about three resting lymphocytes in diameter, round, oval, or spindle shaped, with scant cytoplasm, finely granular salt-and-pepper chromatin, and absent or inconspicuous nucleoli. With so little cytoplasm, neighboring nuclei press into one another, producing nuclear molding. Mitoses are numerous, necrosis is extensive, and the fragile cells are easily crushed in biopsies. As neuroendocrine cells they contain dense-core granules and express chromogranin, synaptophysin, and CD56, which separates them from lymphocytes and from poorly differentiated squamous carcinoma.

Nearly all small cell carcinomas have lost function of both TP53 and RB1. Without these tumor suppressors the cells lose the G1 checkpoint and the normal response to DNA damage, so they divide rapidly while tolerating genomic injury. The result is a very high growth fraction and early spread through lymphatics and blood vessels. Most patients already have metastases at diagnosis, commonly to the liver, bone, brain, and adrenal glands, so the disease behaves as systemic rather than local. It is often staged simply as limited disease, confined to one side of the chest and regional nodes, or extensive disease.

Neuroendocrine differentiation also explains the paraneoplastic syndromes. The cells keep the machinery to make and secrete peptide hormones, so they can release ACTH, causing Cushing syndrome, or ADH, causing the syndrome of inappropriate ADH secretion (SIADH) with hyponatremia. Their neuronal antigens can provoke autoantibodies that cross-react with the nervous system, the basis of Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome and paraneoplastic encephalomyelitis. The mechanisms are explained in PU-14-F.10.

blocks.predict: Small cell carcinoma and typical carcinoid both arise from bronchial neuroendocrine cells and both stain for chromogranin. Why is one usually metastatic at diagnosis while the other rarely spreads?
blocks.explain: Lineage determines markers and secretory ability, but grade determines behavior. Small cell carcinoma has lost TP53 and RB1, divides rapidly, and invades vessels early; typical carcinoid keeps these controls, grows slowly, and stays local for years.
blocks.check: The loss of TP53 and RB1 in this section and the comparison table in PU-14-F.2.

sections.title: Non-small cell carcinomas: squamous cell and large cell

blocks.text: Non-small cell lung carcinoma groups adenocarcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, and large cell carcinoma, together about 85% of lung cancers. They are grouped because they grow and spread more slowly than small cell carcinoma, so a tumor can still be confined to the chest when found. Adenocarcinoma is covered in PU-14-F.1; this section completes the comparison.

Squamous cell carcinoma makes up about 25% to 30% of lung cancers and is strongly linked to smoking. It arises centrally in main or lobar bronchi, where smoke particles deposit heavily. Chronic irritation converts the pseudostratified ciliated epithelium into squamous epithelium (squamous metaplasia), an adaptation that sacrifices mucociliary clearance; continued exposure then produces dysplasia, carcinoma in situ, and invasive carcinoma. The tumor shows squamous features: keratin pearls, individual cells with dense pink keratinized cytoplasm, and intercellular bridges, the desmosomes between cells seen by light microscopy. It expresses p40, p63, and cytokeratin 5/6.

Central location explains early airway symptoms: cough, hemoptysis, and obstruction with atelectasis or postobstructive pneumonia, and the tumor sheds cells that can be found in sputum. Large squamous tumors outgrow their blood supply; the necrotic center liquefies and drains into a bronchus, leaving a cavity with an air-fluid level. Squamous cell carcinoma is also the lung cancer that secretes PTHrP and causes hypercalcemia.

Large cell carcinoma is an undifferentiated malignant epithelial tumor that shows no glandular, squamous, or neuroendocrine differentiation by light microscopy and immunostaining, so it is a diagnosis of exclusion. It consists of sheets of large cells with moderate to abundant cytoplasm, large vesicular nuclei, and prominent nucleoli. It tends to arise peripherally, grows rapidly, and metastasizes early, giving it a poor prognosis. Improved immunostaining has reclassified many former large cell tumors as poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma or squamous carcinoma, so it is now a small fraction of cases.

rows: Present, but most common type in never smokers
Glands, mucin; TTF-1, napsin A; lepidic in AIS
Clubbing and hypertrophic osteoarthropathy; EGFR, ALK, KRAS

blocks.text: Paraneoplastic syndromes act at a distance through hormones, cytokines, or autoantibodies. They may precede discovery of the tumor, and each points to a likely cell type.

Squamous cell carcinoma secretes parathyroid hormone related peptide (PTHrP), which binds the same receptor as PTH. In bone it increases osteoblast expression of RANKL, which activates osteoclasts and releases calcium; in the kidney it increases calcium reabsorption and phosphate excretion. Serum calcium rises and phosphate falls, while native PTH is suppressed by the high calcium. Hypercalcemia causes polyuria, constipation, confusion, and a short QT interval.

Ectopic ACTH from small cell carcinoma drives cortisol production; because levels are high and the course is rapid, patients often show hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis, hypertension, hyperglycemia, proximal weakness, and hyperpigmentation (ACTH stimulates melanocortin receptors on melanocytes) before a full cushingoid appearance develops. Ectopic ADH acts on V2 receptors to insert aquaporin-2 channels in the collecting duct, so water is retained despite low plasma osmolality. Serum sodium falls below about 135 mEq/L (reference about 135 to 145), urine is inappropriately concentrated with sodium usually above about 40 mEq/L, and the patient is euvolemic; severe hyponatremia swells brain cells, causing confusion and seizures.

Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome follows the sequence below, causing proximal weakness, reduced reflexes, and dry mouth. With sustained contraction, calcium accumulates in the terminal and release increases, so strength briefly improves; high-frequency nerve stimulation gives an increasing muscle response.

blocks.title: Small cell carcinoma to Lambert-Eaton syndrome
steps: Tumor cells express P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium channels
Immune response produces antibodies against these channels
Antibodies also bind channels on motor nerve terminals
Less calcium enters with each nerve action potential
Less acetylcholine is released; proximal weakness and hyporeflexia
blocks.caption: Autoantibodies raised against tumor antigens cross-react with the presynaptic membrane.

blocks.text: Hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy (clubbing, periosteal new bone on distal long bones, and arthralgia) is most associated with adenocarcinoma. A leading explanation is that megakaryocytes or platelet clumps escape lung filtration, lodge in fingertip vessels, and release platelet-derived growth factor and vascular endothelial growth factor.

blocks.title: Paraneoplastic syndromes matched to lung cancer type
rows: High calcium, low phosphate, suppressed PTH
Hypokalemic alkalosis, hypertension, hyperpigmentation, high cortisol and ACTH
Euvolemic hyponatremia, concentrated urine, urine sodium high
Proximal weakness improving with effort, hyporeflexia, dry mouth
blocks.caption: Squamous cell secretes PTHrP; small cell secretes peptide hormones and triggers neural autoantibodies.

blocks.title: Worked example: two confused smokers
blocks.text: Two heavy smokers with central lung masses are confused. Patient A: calcium 13.2 mg/dL (reference about 8.5 to 10.5), low phosphate, low PTH. Patient B: sodium 118 mEq/L, low plasma osmolality, urine osmolality above plasma, urine sodium 60 mEq/L, normal volume status. Step 1: in A, high calcium with suppressed PTH means the parathyroids are not the source, and low phosphate fits a PTH-like hormone acting on the kidney: PTHrP from squamous cell carcinoma. Step 2: in B, the kidney concentrates urine while plasma is dilute, so ADH is acting without an osmotic stimulus; with euvolemia this is SIADH from small cell carcinoma. Both tumors are central, so the laboratory pattern, not location, separates them.

blocks.predict: A patient with a hilar mass has proximal leg weakness. Would you expect strength to improve or worsen during several seconds of maximal effort?
blocks.explain: Improve. In Lambert-Eaton syndrome the defect is reduced calcium entry into the nerve terminal; repeated firing lets calcium accumulate and increases acetylcholine release. In myasthenia gravis the defect is postsynaptic, so weakness worsens with use.

sections.title: Local effects of lung cancer spread

blocks.text: Local signs of a lung tumor reveal its position. The superior sulcus is the groove for the subclavian vessels at the lung apex. A superior sulcus (Pancoast) tumor, usually a non-small cell carcinoma, grows out of the apex into the thoracic inlet, where it meets the lower trunk of the brachial plexus (C8 and T1 roots), the cervical sympathetic chain and stellate ganglion, the subclavian vessels, and the upper ribs.

Invasion of C8 and T1 causes shoulder pain radiating along the medial arm, forearm, and ulnar side of the hand, with weakness and wasting of the intrinsic hand muscles. Invasion of the sympathetic chain interrupts the pathway shown below and produces Horner syndrome on the same side: ptosis from loss of sympathetic tone to the superior tarsal muscle, miosis from unopposed parasympathetic constriction of the pupil, and anhidrosis of the face. Rib destruction adds severe local pain.

blocks.title: Sympathetic pathway to the eye interrupted at the lung apex
steps: Hypothalamic neurons descend to the ciliospinal center (C8 to T2)
Preganglionic fibers exit mainly at T1 and cross the lung apex
Fibers ascend in the sympathetic chain to the superior cervical ganglion
Postganglionic fibers follow the carotid arteries to the eye and face
Apical tumor cuts the chain: ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis
blocks.caption: The preganglionic fibers pass directly over the pleural dome, so apical tumors interrupt them.

blocks.text: The superior vena cava is a thin-walled, low-pressure vein in the right side of the mediastinum, easily compressed or invaded by right-sided central tumors and nodes, most often small cell carcinoma, and also by lymphoma. Venous return from the head, neck, and arms backs up, causing a swollen, plethoric face, distended neck and chest wall collateral veins, arm edema, headache, and dyspnea.

The left recurrent laryngeal nerve loops beneath the aortic arch beside the ligamentum arteriosum and then ascends in the groove between trachea and esophagus, so a left hilar tumor or enlarged nodes beneath the aortic arch can paralyze it. The right nerve hooks around the subclavian artery higher in the neck and is involved less often. Loss of the nerve paralyzes all intrinsic laryngeal muscles except the cricothyroid, so the fold on that side cannot close fully and the voice becomes hoarse and breathy. The phrenic nerve (C3 to C5) descends anterior to the lung root on each side; invasion paralyzes the hemidiaphragm, which is elevated on imaging and moves paradoxically upward during a sniff.

blocks.title: Structures invaded by lung cancer and the resulting signs
rows: Horner syndrome on the same side
Ulnar-side arm pain, intrinsic hand weakness
Facial plethora and swelling, distended neck veins, arm edema
Left hilum, below the aortic arch
blocks.caption: Local signs map the tumor onto thoracic anatomy.

blocks.predict: A smoker with a right apical mass has a small right pupil and a drooping right eyelid. Will the right side of the forehead sweat normally?
blocks.explain: No. The tumor interrupts preganglionic fibers before they reach the superior cervical ganglion, so the postganglionic fibers to the facial sweat glands, which travel with the external carotid branches, lose their input and the face is dry on that side.

sections.title: Metastases to the lung and pulmonary hamartoma

blocks.text: The lung is among the most common sites of metastasis, and metastatic tumors in the lung outnumber primary lung cancers. The reason is circulatory: the lungs receive the entire systemic venous return through the pulmonary arteries, and their capillary bed acts as a filter for tumor cells released from almost any organ drained by the systemic veins. Tumors also reach the lung through lymphatics.

Blood-borne metastases appear as multiple, round, well-circumscribed nodules of varying size, often in both lungs and more numerous in the periphery and lower zones, where blood flow is greatest. Very large round deposits are called cannonball metastases. Common primaries include carcinomas of the breast, colon, and kidney, and sarcomas. A different pattern, lymphangitic spread, fills the lymphatics with tumor and produces thickened interstitial lines rather than round nodules.

A solitary pulmonary nodule is a single round opacity of 3 cm or less surrounded by lung; a larger lesion is called a mass. Causes include primary lung cancer, a single metastasis, infectious granulomas from tuberculosis or endemic fungi, and benign tumors such as hamartoma. Small size, smooth margins, no growth over about 2 years, and benign calcification patterns (central, diffuse, laminated, or popcorn) favor a benign cause. Larger size, spiculated margins, upper lobe location, growth, smoking, and older age favor malignancy.

Pulmonary hamartoma is the most common benign lung tumor. Its name implies a disorganized overgrowth of native tissue, but it is a true benign neoplasm with clonal chromosomal rearrangements, often involving the HMGA2 gene. It is usually a peripheral, well-circumscribed, round nodule, most often a few centimeters or less, found incidentally in an adult. Microscopically it contains lobules of mature hyaline cartilage mixed with fat, fibrous tissue, and clefts lined by respiratory epithelium. The cartilage calcifies in clumps, producing popcorn calcification on imaging, and fat within the nodule on CT is nearly diagnostic.

sections.title: HPV-related and tobacco-related squamous cell carcinoma of the head and neck

blocks.text: Squamous cell carcinoma is the dominant cancer of the oral cavity and pharynx, but it has two distinct causes that produce two different diseases. The classic form follows tobacco, smoked or chewed (including betel quid), and alcohol, which act synergistically. Carcinogens such as polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons and nitrosamines cause mutations, most often in TP53, across the whole exposed mucosa. This field cancerization explains why these patients often have precursor lesions, leukoplakia (a white patch) and the higher-risk erythroplakia (a red patch), and why second primary tumors of the upper aerodigestive tract and lung are common. Typical sites are the lateral tongue, floor of the mouth, larynx, and hypopharynx, mainly in older men.

HPV-related carcinoma arises in the oropharynx, mainly the palatine tonsils and the base of the tongue (lingual tonsil). These sites have deep crypts lined by reticulated epithelium, a thin, discontinuous lining infiltrated by lymphoid cells that is thought to give the virus access to basal cells. HPV 16 causes the large majority of cases. Infection is acquired sexually, including through oral sex, and patients tend to be younger and are often nonsmokers.

blocks.caption: p16 overexpression is the routine marker of an HPV-driven oropharyngeal carcinoma.

blocks.text: Because E7 disables Rb, the normal feedback that limits p16 is lost and p16 accumulates, so strong p16 staining serves as a surrogate marker for HPV-driven tumors. Because the virus inactivates p53 and Rb at the protein level, these tumors usually lack TP53 mutations, unlike tobacco-related tumors.

The two forms present differently. HPV-positive tumors often have a small primary with early, enlarged, frequently cystic neck node metastases, so a painless neck mass is a common first sign, and they carry a better prognosis than tobacco-related tumors. Tobacco-related tumors more often present as a visible ulcer or mass with pain and are more likely to be accompanied by a second primary.

integration.text: Anatomy and histology explain where each tumor arises and what it does next. Central bronchi carry the heaviest smoke exposure and contain the squamous metaplasia and neuroendocrine cells that give rise to squamous and small cell carcinoma, while peripheral alveolar epithelium gives rise to adenocarcinoma. The neighbors of each site predict the signs: the sympathetic chain and brachial plexus at the apex, the superior vena cava and recurrent laryngeal nerve in the mediastinum, the eustachian tube beside the nasopharynx, and the trachea beside the esophagus. Microbiology and immunology add two virus-driven pathways, EBV in the nasopharynx and HPV in the tonsils and larynx, which differ in how strongly their oncoproteins disable p53 and Rb, and paraneoplastic autoimmunity in which antibodies against tumor antigens attack nerve terminals.

Biochemistry and physiology explain the systemic findings: PTHrP mimics PTH, ectopic ADH concentrates urine against a dilute plasma, and loss of presynaptic calcium entry reduces acetylcholine release. These rules have limits. Markers support rather than prove a diagnosis and must be read as a panel, many tumors are mixed or poorly differentiated, percentages for each lung cancer type shift with smoking patterns and classification changes, and an adenocarcinoma in a smoker or a squamous carcinoma in a nonsmoker remains entirely possible.

summary: Adenocarcinoma is the most common lung cancer overall and in never smokers and women; it is peripheral, gland forming, mucin producing, and TTF-1 positive.
Adenocarcinoma in situ shows pure lepidic growth along intact alveolar walls, 3 cm or less, with no stromal, vascular, or pleural invasion.
Squamous cell and small cell carcinomas are central and strongly smoking related; adenocarcinoma and large cell carcinoma are peripheral.

Squamous cell carcinoma shows keratin pearls and intercellular bridges, may cavitate, and secretes PTHrP; small cell carcinoma shows nuclear molding, expresses chromogranin and synaptophysin, loses TP53 and RB1, and metastasizes early.
Small cell carcinoma secretes ACTH and ADH and triggers Lambert-Eaton antibodies against presynaptic P/Q-type calcium channels; hypertrophic osteoarthropathy is most associated with adenocarcinoma.
Bronchial carcinoid is a low-grade neuroendocrine endobronchial tumor without a smoking link that obstructs bronchi and rarely causes carcinoid syndrome.
Pancoast tumors cause Horner syndrome and C8 to T1 deficits; central tumors cause superior vena cava syndrome, recurrent laryngeal hoarseness, and phrenic paralysis.
Mesothelioma follows asbestos exposure by decades, is not related to smoking, encases the lung, and is calretinin positive with long slender microvilli.
Metastases outnumber primary lung cancers and form multiple round nodules; hamartoma is a single nodule of cartilage and fat with popcorn calcification.

Nasopharyngeal carcinoma is EBV related and presents with neck nodes or one-sided serous otitis media; HPV 16 causes p16-positive tonsil and base of tongue carcinoma, while tobacco and alcohol cause TP53-mutated oral and laryngeal carcinoma.

verify: Percentages for each lung cancer type (adenocarcinoma about 40% or more, squamous cell about 25% to 30%, small cell about 15%, carcinoid a few percent) vary by source and year; confirm the figures NABNE expects, especially for large cell carcinoma, which older sources give as about 10%.

Size thresholds for adenocarcinoma in situ (3 cm or less) and minimally invasive adenocarcinoma (invasion 5 mm or less) follow the current WHO classification; confirm NABNE uses the same terms and no longer expects bronchioloalveolar carcinoma.
The age profile of bronchial carcinoid and the frequency of carcinoid syndrome with bronchial carcinoids are reported differently across sources; this chapter states them qualitatively.
Asbestos latency for mesothelioma is quoted from about 20 to more than 40 years; confirm the range NABNE uses.
Mesothelioma immunohistochemistry panels evolve (calretinin, WT1, D2-40, cytokeratin 5/6 versus CEA, MOC-31, BerEP4, claudin-4, TTF-1); confirm which markers NABNE expects.
The WHO classification of nasopharyngeal carcinoma also lists a basaloid squamous subtype, omitted here; confirm whether NABNE tests the subtypes beyond keratinizing versus nonkeratinizing.
The platelet and megakaryocyte growth factor mechanism of hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy is a leading hypothesis, not a settled mechanism.
Urine sodium cutoff for SIADH (above about 40 mEq/L) and the hypercalcemia example values use common teaching thresholds; laboratory reference ranges vary.
Confirm whether NABNE expects the eponyms Pancoast tumor and Lambert-Eaton syndrome, or only the descriptive terms.
